pr_title: Add option to the JSON.NET output formatter
pr_body:
- Add an option to increase the buffer threshold for writing to the output. We have several long standing performance issues with the JSON.NET output formatter and this addresses one of them by making the buffer threshold before going to disk configurable.

Fixes #17843

PS: There are other performance issues with the FileBuffering*Streams but this doesn't try to address those. We have [another issue](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/21245) for that

issue_context.title: High disk IO volume after upgrading to 3.0
comments: @rynowak @richlander
Starting with `area-servers`
Probably the buffering in the legacy MVC response serializers (e.g. Newtonsoft.Json). @pranavkm

We tried downgrading to 2.2 and the disk write came down to 0 bytes. And yes we are using Newtonsoft.Json. we used newtonsoft.json with both 2.2 and 3.0

Does this mean that using newtonsoft + 3.0 is likely to result in high disk write volume?
Disabling SuppressOutputFormatterBuffering will also require enabling AllowSynchronousIO on the server. https://github.com/aspnet/Announcements/issues/342

Thanks for the response. 
> In 3.0 and newer by default the newtonsoft.json serializer will buffer into memory (up to 32kb) and then to disk if the payload is larger than that.

is 32kb configurable? any downside in increasing it? response from my service is less than 2MB. 

We were talking about switching to `System.Text.Json`. it requires quite a bit of work but we will get to the new json api.
If you *really* wanted to get fancy, you could write an action filter that set `ObjectResult.Formatters` to include just the S.T.J formatter, and then you could progressively migrate that way.

@nur858 - for us to look into this, is there any reason in particular where you're trying to avoid disk writes? Is there something else about your scenario/environment where disk ends up as a scarce resource? Trying to find info so we can investigate effectively.

I have a large fleet of containers running in the cloud serving a high traffic service. But large amount of disk writes saturated available IO bandwidth causing kernel panic.The service is a thin layer on top of cache and we were getting consistent response time with .net 2.2  but since we upgraded to 3.0, the response time got very spiky with certain percentage of timeouts. 

Would it be possible to use dedicated memory pool for output buffering when using newtonsoft instead of disk? This is clearly making kestrel a poor choice for high throughput service.

Thanks for that detail @nur858! We’re working on a workaround for you. There are a bunch but we’re looking for the one with the best tradeoffs. 

> Would it be possible to use dedicated memory pool for output buffering when using newtonsoft instead of disk? This is clearly making kestrel a poor choice for high throughput service.

The issues is that newtonsoft.json does blocking IO (which we disabled in 3.0) and we worked around This with disk buffering. The new JSON serializer is fully asynchronous and doesn’t have this problem but I assume you changed back to newtonsoft because of some missing features, we hope to improve that going forward.

There are some things to improve here regardless. Thanks for your patience!

Thanks @davidfowl.  that's very good news. We ran into similar predicament before  with newtonsoft. But we chose to stick to it for couple of reasons:
1. It's popularity and familiarity among developers
2. Reluctance to try a brand new API 
3. it was already being used by other services
 
Async serializer is clearly preferred choice but I am pretty sure there is appetite for using newtonsoft.json with 3.0 considering this is one of the most popular .net package out there. 

Thanks everyone for prompt response!!
@nur858 Do you have an idea of how big your response sizes are? I'm trying to decide if you're better off with a solution that just bumps up the buffer size.
@davidfowl yeah. largest response is ~2MB

Has there been any progress on this issue?
We’ve likely also run into this issue, as upgrading to .NET Core 3.x came with serious performance hits, and we have a similar setup of large JSON responses (~600kb) and reliance on newtonsoft due to heavy use of jsonconverters helping with deserialising a very hierarchical object system.

We’d love to use STJ, but it doesn’t seem advanced enough to support our use case yet.

Is there any documentation on using a particular serialiser only for serialising you response (without having to manually do it in the controller)?

@Systemic33 there isn't a built in way in MVC to configure a formatter per controller \ action. The closest would be to use content-types to perform selection. That said, you could write a formatter that delegates to one of the System.Text.Json or Newtonsoft.Json based formatters based on the presence of some metadata on the action descriptor.

> @Systemic33 there isn't a built in way in MVC to configure a formatter per controller \ action. The closest would be to use content-types to perform selection. That said, you could write a formatter that delegates to one of the System.Text.Json or Newtonsoft.Json based formatters based on the presence of some metadata on the action descriptor.

You could use a result filter to manipulate `ObjectResult`. https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/src/Mvc/Mvc.Core/src/ObjectResult.cs#L26
@pranavkm did we do anything in this area for 5.0?
Seems we missed the output buffering configuration options. I just checked and we only exposed a configurable threshold for the input buffer size 😭. We need to tackle this in 6.0

That's very unfortunate.

We currently mitigate/workaround this by forcing Kestrel back to synchronised request pipeline together with Newtonsoft JSON. Effectively running as if .NET Core 2.x.
The API only has internal services as users, so we can accept the issues that come with that.
@Systemic33 , exactly how did you do this? Facing slow serialization performance in a project when returning a 1-2Mb sized response.

If the slowness is due to disk IO and you are using newtonSoft.Json then you can try [enabling synchronous IO](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.server.kestrel.core.kestrelserveroptions.allowsynchronousio?view=aspnetcore-5.0)
